extracted.intended_audience: judges, patent attorneys, law students, and patent litigators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging the adequacy, construction, and scope of patent specifications and for deciding infringement and related procedural questions (court vs. jury roles, evidence, and jurisdiction). Applies to litigation and statutory interpretation of patent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory requirement to specify and point out the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act of Congress requires, that he 'shall, particularly, specify and point the part, improvement, or combination, which he claims as his own invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory duty underpins the need for reasonable certainty in the description so the public can know whether they violate the patent and can practice the invention when the term expires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of description to enable competent workman (practicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sufficiency of the description, to enable competent persons to apply the invention, is a question of fact for the jury, on the testimony of experts and the language itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury determines whether the directions are sufficiently clear and explicit to enable a competent workman to practise the invention, after being informed by the court what the specification has said. The court may need to instruct the jury as to the specification's contents; words of art or surrounding circumstances that affect meaning may require evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court declares what the specification has said (construction is for the court)
rubrics_metrics.description: The court is to declare what the specification has said; the meaning of the specification is for the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the jury decides sufficiency/practicability, the court must construe the specification (a question of law) and may take into view uncontroverted evidence bearing on meaning. If words of art or surrounding circumstances affect meaning, the court will instruct conditionally (dependent on facts found by the jury).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of jury in interpreting words of art and surrounding circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The aid of the jury will be required to ascertain the meaning of words of art, or the surrounding circumstances, which govern that meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When meaning depends on technical terms or extrinsic circumstances, the court tells the jury 'the specification has said so and so' according to the jury's findings on those facts; the jury then decides whether directions would mislead a workman or are sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence may affect construction but cannot supply positive omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: The court should receive and watch the evidence, and to apply it to the construction, taking care that it be not allowed to go so far as to supply positive omissions, which would render the specification defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff may offer evidence to show specification meaning; evidence can affect construction but must not be used to fill in material omissions from the specification itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal construction in favour of inventors (but within sound principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: A liberal construction is to be given to a patent, and inventors sustained, if practicable, without a departure from sound principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifications should be sustained if they can fairly be read to cover the invention; courts should not be astute to avoid inventions. This encourages ingenuity but must not depart from legal principles or allow vague or insufficient claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical approach to construction (avoid metaphysical distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters like these must be received in a practical manner, and not decided on mere metaphysical distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructions should be consistent with drawings, express language, the chief object of the machine, and practicability; the court may infer intended scope from the whole specification and drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of specification vs. intelligibility/practicability are separable
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of what the specification has said (construction) is for the court; the intelligibility of the practical directions (sufficiency to carry into effect) is for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although these issues may arise from the same passages, courts should separate the legal construction from factual questions about whether the specification enables practice of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether invention is a patentable subject is a question of law
rubrics_metrics.description: The question whether the invention disclosed by the specification is a proper subject for a patent is a question of law, on which the court will instruct the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is distinct from novelty (a question of fact). Even if an invention is new, the court must decide whether it is the kind of subject that the patent law recognizes (e.g., mere new use of known thing may not be patentable subject matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and identity (infringement) are questions of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelty of the invention is a pre-requisite to validity and is a question of fact; the question of infringement (identity) is a matter of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement requires factual determination whether the defendant's thing is 'substantially the same' as the plaintiff's invention; the jury decides under proper legal instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff may assert specification requires explanation of facts to determine extent of claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff is always entitled to say, that his specification requires the explanation of facts, to determine the extent of his claim and the character of his invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court should receive evidence to ascertain whether such explanation is needed, but watch that evidence does not supply essential omissions. The construction (meaning) may be affected by evidence where the court has no judicial knowledge of technical terms or circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of drawings, language, and declared objects to construe claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Looking to the whole specification and drawing, both the figure and language, [the court asks] could any one doubt that [a particular embodiment] was intended to be used in the new combination which was patented?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may rely on drawings, explicit descriptions, and the inventor's stated objectives (e.g., increased velocity) to resolve ambiguities and determine which embodiments the patentee intended to claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional power and retroactive grants — avoid retrospective operation if possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has power to pass an act which will operate retrospectively to give a patent for an invention which is already in public use; but no act ought to be construed to operate retrospectively, unless such a construction is unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Congress' power is broad (can grant retrospective patents), courts prefer constructions that avoid creating retrospective liabilities for acts lawful when done; interpret ambiguous statutory language to avoid retroactivity where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal jurisdiction over patent actions (exclusive jurisdiction of federal courts)
rubrics_metrics.description: All actions, suits, controversies, and cases arising under any law of the United States, granting or confirming to inventors the exclusive right to their inventions or discoveries, shall be originally cognizable ... by the Circuit courts of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circuit courts have power in law and equity on patent matters (including injunctions). It is the better opinion that this jurisdiction is exclusive and state courts cannot entertain patent infringement suits or declare patents void.
